title: Build and inspect strings
summary: Replace topic with "moon" before these two operations. What prints?
explanation: An interpolated string begins with $. Expressions inside braces are evaluated and inserted into the text, as in $"Score: {score}".

A string value is immutable. Methods such as ToUpperInvariant return another string; they do not rewrite the original variable’s value unless you assign that result.

ToUpperInvariant() takes no arguments and returns an uppercased string using invariant culture: fixed casing rules rather than the user’s current language settings. The receiver remains unchanged; a distinct new string object is not promised.

Length counts UTF-16 code units. An index in brackets starts at zero; text[0] reads the first code unit as a char. Some displayed characters use more than one code unit, so Length is not always a count of human-visible symbols.
Calling a method and ignoring its result leaves the original text unchanged. Store the returned value if you need it later.
Expected behavior from this example: stars / STARS. This expected result is a reasoned prediction until a compiler test is recorded.

title: Await an asynchronous operation
summary: ReadMinutesAsync now returns 7 instead of 4. What is printed, and when?
explanation: Task<T> represents an operation that will produce a T or fail. async permits await inside the method; it does not automatically create a new thread.

await waits for completion without blocking a thread just to wait for an incomplete task. The continuation uses the resulting value after completion.

Task.Delay(10) takes a delay in milliseconds and returns a Task representing that delay. Awaiting it does not block a thread just to wait; scheduling means continuation is not promised at an exact instant.
An exception from an asynchronous Task method is observed when awaiting its task. Prefer Task rather than async void for ordinary methods so the caller can await and handle completion.

title: Transfer resources with move semantics
summary: If b is copied from a instead, why does the final output still read 2 7?

title: Use diagnostics and sanitizers responsibly
summary: With this course’s -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror flags, add int unused = 7; inside main and never use it. What should you do with the build result?
explanation:
Use -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic to request useful GCC diagnostics. They do not mean every possible warning is enabled. This course also uses -Werror, which treats emitted warnings as build errors rather than silently accepting them.

Save the complete safe example below as main.cpp in a disposable folder. With GCC installed, these terminal commands build it with the stated warning policy and then run it on Linux or macOS:
```sh
g++ -std=c++23 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror main.cpp -o example
./example
```
The output is 2 4. These commands do not install a compiler.

A local build with -g -fsanitize=address,undefined can instrument checks for supported memory and undefined-behavior errors. It only checks paths that actually execute; a clean run does not prove the whole program safe. Tool availability and platform support matter.

On a platform whose GCC supports these sanitizers, build the same safe source into a separate executable:
```sh
g++ -std=c++23 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -g -fsanitize=address,undefined main.cpp -o checked
./checked
```
Its normal program output is still 2 4; sanitizer diagnostics, if any, must be investigated. A platform limitation is not a passing safety test.

The worked array iteration stays in bounds. We do not execute invalid indexing or dangling-pointer examples. To demonstrate a rejected build safely, the changed case adds a genuinely unused variable; the configured warning policy rejects it before any run.
Expected output or behavior: 2 4 . Local compiler test evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

title: Update a simple counter atomically

count.load() takes no arguments and atomically returns the current counter value without changing it. This call uses the same default sequentially consistent ordering as the fetch-add calls.

This example keeps the default sequentially consistent ordering. It does not teach custom memory-order or lock-free design. Individual atomic variables do not automatically preserve a multi-variable invariant; mutex-protected groups of operations may still be needed.

title: Mutex-protected shared state
summary: If both loop bounds change from 1000 to 250, what is the final count?
explanation: The file-scope static int count has static storage duration and is initialized to zero even without a written initializer. count++ reads and writes shared state; a mutex must protect the entire operation. Initialize the mutex before starting work. Join the worker before reading the final count and destroying the mutex. The cast (void)unused explicitly discards the required callback argument. Checked failures abort rather than continuing unprotected; failed thread creation destroys the initialized mutex.

mtx_unlock(&lock) releases that same mutex after the protected update; it returns thrd_success on success. The calling thread must own the lock before unlocking it.

title: Atomic counters and memory order

atomic_int and atomic_fetch_add come from optional C atomics. atomic_init initializes the counter before any concurrent use. Each fetch-add is one atomic read-modify-write and returns the previous value, which this example intentionally ignores.
